issues.item: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, avoiding open spaces due to feeling physically vulnerable suggests a different threat context (e.g., assault, combat, public attack) and is not clinically well integrated with the other selected items, which are grief-related. Within the Maladaptive Strategies node, 'Avoid Positive Feelings' and 'Avoid Grief Reminders' are coherent with bereavement-related PTSD, but 'Avoid Open Spaces' pulls toward a conflicting trauma/symptom pattern that is hard to explain from the provided formulation and item set.

vignette: Emmett Hernandez sat at his pottery wheel, hands hesitating over the lump of clay in front of him. It had been months since he'd last created anything worthwhile, and even longer since his wife, Maria, had passed away. He couldn't shake the feeling that every time he tried to get back into his craft, he was somehow betraying her memory. The smell of damp earth and clay usually brought him comfort, but now it only served as a harsh reminder of all the things they used to do together. As he struggled to focus on the task at hand, Emmett's mind began to wander back to the day Maria died. He remembered the hospital room, the beeping machines, and the numbness that had washed over him when the doctor delivered the news. It was as if time had stood still in that moment, and everything since then had been a blur. The grief felt like a weight he couldn't shake, always lurking just beneath the surface. Emmett found himself pushing away any positive emotions that dared to creep in. When friends or family tried to console him with stories of Maria's warmth and kindness, he'd change the subject or politely excuse himself. It wasn't that he didn't appreciate their efforts; it was just that allowing himself to feel good – even for a moment – felt like he was somehow diminishing his love for her. Avoiding anything that reminded him of Maria had become second nature. Emmett would take detours on his daily walks to avoid passing by the park where they used to picnic, and he'd stopped attending pottery classes because the instructor's voice sounded too much like Maria's. Even small things, like cooking his favorite meals or listening to their shared playlist, felt like a betrayal. Making plans for the future had also become impossible. Emmett would get anxious at the mere suggestion of booking a vacation or planning a project beyond the next few days. What was the point, anyway? Without Maria by his side, everything felt uncertain and scary. His friends and family tried to reassure him that life went on, but Emmett couldn't shake the feeling that he was just going through the motions. As the weeks turned into months, Emmett's avoidance behaviors had started to take a toll on his relationships. His children were worried about him, his friends felt like they'd lost touch, and even his pottery wheel gathered dust in the corner of the room. It was as if Emmett had built a wall around himself, and he didn't know how to tear it down. One day, as he sat amidst the silence of his studio, Emmett realized that he couldn't keep living like this. The pain wasn't going away, but maybe – just maybe – it was time to start facing it head-on. With a newfound sense of determination, he slowly began to clean up his workspace and prepare for a new project. It wouldn't be easy, but for the first time in months, Emmett felt like he might finally be ready to take the next step forward.
